newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong returns to China, to keep old lifestyle.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong returns to China, to keep old lifestyle.

text.p: Britain's heir to the throne Prince Charles on Monday handed Hong Kong, its 6.4 million people and its capitalist treasures to China's President Jiang Zemin, head of the last great communist party on earth.
To the strains of God Save the Queen, the Union Jack was lowered on the final glittering possession of the British empire at the stroke of midnight.
In its place rose the red five-star flag of the People's Republic of China and the bauhinia flower standard of the new Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR).
Beijing has pledged that the region may keep its freewheeling capitalist lifestyle for another 50 years under a "one country, two systems" formula negotiated with Britain.

The new chief executive Tung Chee-hwa, 60, a Shanghai-born shipping magnate, was sworn in by Chinese Premier Li Peng along with a Beijing-picked legislature that replaced a democratically-elected body.
Chris Patten, the 28th and last governor who preferred a business suit to the plumed hat and ceremonial sword of office, bowed out with a terse telegram to the London Foreign Office.
"I have relinquished the administration of this Government. God Save the Queen," read his despatch, signed "Patten".
"We shall not forget you," Charles declared to the people of Hong Kong moments before he returned the Pearl of the Orient to Jiang, a Soviet-trained engineer.

Jiang said: "July 1, 1997 will go down in the annals of history as a day that merits eternal memory." From now on, he proclaimed, "Hong Kong compatriots have become true masters of this Chinese land".

Earlier, a cavalcade of open-backed trucks and buses carrying 509 lightly-armed Chinese troops -- ordered to "love the people of Hong Kong" -- moved into the city as the departing Britons staged an end-of-empire extravaganza.
They drove quickly to the Prince of Wales barracks in the city centre, new headquarters of the People's Liberation Army.
A second and major wave of 4,000 troops backed by armour, helicopters and warships was set to sweep in at dawn to fully assert Chinese sovereignty.

With Charles at his side, Patten -- whose crusade for democracy in the twilight of colonial rule earned him Beijing's abiding hatred as a "whore" and "villain" -- showered kisses on well-wishers at the dockside of Victoria Harbour before stepping up the gangway of the royal yacht Britannia.
As the vessel slipped its moorings, the first stirrings of opposition to new Chinese rule took shape.
Leading democracy campaigner Martin Lee made good on a threat to denounce the new legislature from the balcony of the building where its doomed colonial predecessor sat.
"We pledge to continue to be the voice of Hong Kong people -- in or out of office -- and to fight to get democracy back," the barrister-turned-activist told a crowd of thousands.
Nearby, firebrand politician Emily Lau told at least 1,000 demonstrators packed into Statue Square: "The message is that we want democracy and we want it now".
Other protesters carried banners reading "Down with Li Peng", and "Remember the June 4 slaughter", a reference to the 1989 Tiananmen massacre in Beijing that sparked fear and revulsion in Hong Kong.
Tung, a billionaire whose Chinese name means "build China", has promised popular elections for a new legislature next May.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright boycotted the swearing-in ceremony of the chief executive, lawmakers, the judiciary and top civil servants.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said he expected China would be obliged to allow some "dissent".
"The agreement says that there will be one China and two systems. And it's hard to have a system with free elections and freedom of speech and open press without dissent.
"I can't imagine how you could have it any other way."
Under a tropical downpour at sunset, Britain bade farewell to Hong Kong. A last exuberant hurrah featured bagpipers, opera divas, dragon dancers and massed choirs.

A crowd of 10,000 huddled under umbrellas while more than 100 million television viewers around the world witnessed the pomp and pageantry of Britain's retreat from a territory seized from the Celestial Kingdom.

High above the harbour, in the headquarters penthouse of Jardine Matheson, whose taipans run the conglomerate known as the "Princely Hong", young executives and their girlfriends slurped champagne and writhed to disco music.
Their buccaneering forebears, William Jardine and James Matheson, ran an opium trade which led to war between Britain and China and the capture of Hong Kong at gunpoint in 1841.
The night sky over the harbour turned flaming red with cascading fireworks, illuminating Britannia and its escort frigate HMS Chatham.

At a sumptuous banquet at the Hong Kong convention centre Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen proposed a toast to Jiang, Britain's Queen Elizabeth and the "long-term stability and prosperity of Hong Kong".
In the final hours of British rule, Britain and China began patching up a row over democratic reforms.

Jiang, the only Chinese head of state to set foot in Hong Kong, met British Prime Minister Tony Blair for the first time and invited him to China. Blair accepted and urged Jiang to forget past battles and build a new relationship.
The Chinese president flew in with Zhuo Lin, widow of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who had died four months before he could fulfil a lifelong wish to see the reunification.

In Beijing, Tiananmen Square was a blaze of neon light and colour as dancers and folk singers on a vast stage entertained a crowd of 100,000 celebrating an event that banners proclaimed would "wash away 100 years of shame".
For China, the return of Hong Kong to the motherland and the departure of the last colonists from its shores erased an era of humiliation.
But the swift dispatch of troops has angered Hong Kong democrats, who still have nightmares over Tiananmen.
Half an hour before Jiang's Air China flight touched down, Patten was swept from Government House in a black Rolls Royce to the strains of "Auld Lang Syne".

Patten, 53, choked back tears, and his wife and three daughters were misty-eyed, as a police bugler played the Last Post on the lawns of the colonial mansion and the Union Jack was lowered and wrapped up for him to take away.

Wearing a ceremonial sword at the harbour festivities, Prince Charles read a message from his mother Queen Elizabeth, in which she stressed Hong Kong's future depended on faithful implementation by Beijing of the 1984 Sino-British agreement.

Patten, rain soaking his suit, fought tears after an ovation for his farewell speech when he declared that Hong Kong's "unshakeable destiny" was to run its own affairs. No dependent territory had ever achieved more prosperity, he said.

Then the former governor and his family, Prince Charles at their side, waved tearfully from the railings of the Britannia as it eased past brightly-lit marble skyscrapers lining the harbour and headed into the South China Sea.
